blocks.text: Sickle cell disease is an **inherited haemoglobinopathy**. One amino-acid change in the β-globin chain produces **haemoglobin S (HbS)**, which distorts red cells into rigid, fragile sickle shapes. The result is a lifelong **haemolytic anaemia** with recurrent episodes of small-vessel blockage, called "crises".

blocks.title: Molecular basis
items: A single-base change (adenine → thymine) in the β-globin gene on **chromosome 11** alters codon 6
**Valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6** of the β chain: a neutral residue takes the place of a negatively charged one
The charge change alters how the haemoglobin migrates, which is the basis of diagnosis by **Hb electrophoresis**
Compare HbC: the same position 6, but **lysine** replaces glutamic acid

blocks.title: Autosomal recessive inheritance
rows: Only abnormal β chains: HbS, no HbA
A mixture of HbA and HbS

blocks.title: Epidemiology
items: Heterozygote (carrier) rate is **over 20% in tropical Africa**; about **8%** of Black Americans carry the trait
Also found in India, the Middle East and around the Mediterranean
The distribution mirrors **falciparum malaria**: carriers are less likely to die of falciparum malaria in early childhood, a **balanced polymorphism** that keeps the gene common
Homozygotes get **no extra** malaria protection

blocks.note: Look at: world map of haemoglobinopathies. Sickle-cell anaemia clusters in tropical Africa, overlapping the malaria belt.

blocks.text: β-chain disorders appear only **after about 6 months of age**. Until then most haemoglobin is fetal HbF (α2γ2), which has no β chains and does not sickle.
Zero to Finals says HbF is replaced by HbA at around 6 weeks, but Davidson's and Kumar & Clark place the onset of β-chain disease **after about 6 months**. Use 6 months in the exam.

When HbS loses its oxygen it becomes insoluble and **polymerises into rigid pseudocrystals ("tactoids")**. These stretch the membrane into the sickle shape. At first, re-oxygenation reverses the change. After many cycles the membrane loses its flexibility and the cell stays **irreversibly sickled**.

blocks.title: Why cells become irreversibly sickled
items: Potassium escapes through the calcium-activated **Gardos channel**, and water follows
The cell becomes dehydrated and dense, which concentrates HbS. The higher the HbS concentration, the faster tactoids form
These dense cells stay sickled even when oxygen returns

blocks.title: Two consequences of sickling
rows: Rigid cells are removed early (shortened red cell survival)
Chronic anaemia, jaundice, reticulocytosis, pigment gallstones
Sickled cells plug the microcirculation; endothelial adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 may help trap them
Tissue infarction: painful crises and chronic organ damage

blocks.title: Precipitants of sickling
items: Hypoxia (e.g. altitude, unpressurised flight)
Infection and fever
Dehydration
Acidosis
Cold
Often no trigger is found. Mnemonic: **"HIDe in the COLD"**

blocks.title: Other haemoglobins modify polymerisation
rows: High HbF means a milder course with few crises. This is why hydroxycarbamide (which raises HbF) works
HbSC gives real (if milder) disease, unlike HbAS
Trait cells sickle only under extreme hypoxia

blocks.text: HbS **releases oxygen to the tissues more easily** than HbA. Patients therefore tolerate a steady-state Hb of 60–80 g/L with few anaemic symptoms outside crises.

sections.title: Sickle syndromes and sickle cell trait

blocks.title: Sickle syndromes
rows: Full picture: haemolysis, crises and multi-organ damage
Like HbSS (can be just as severe)
HbS co-inherited with a β-thalassaemia gene
Fewer crises, but more **retinopathy** and **thrombosis**, and more problems in pregnancy
Normal blood count and film; see below

blocks.text: **Sickle cell trait (HbAS)**: one normal β gene, so the cells contain both HbA and HbS. Carriers are not anaemic, have a **normal blood count and film** and a normal life expectancy, and need no treatment. Sickling happens only with **extreme hypoxia**, such as flying in an unpressurised aircraft.

blocks.title: Sickle cell trait: points to remember
items: Protects young children from dying of **falciparum malaria**, but a carrier still needs antimalarial prophylaxis when travelling
Renal medulla: cannot concentrate urine (**isosthenuria / hyposthenuria**), haematuria from papillary necrosis, more UTIs
Davidson's: more **unexplained non-visible haematuria**
Davidson's: once thought harmless, the trait may carry a **higher risk of sudden and cardiovascular death**
Diagnosis is by a positive sickle test or by **Hb electrophoresis**. Screening allows genetic counselling

blocks.text: If **both partners carry the trait**, each pregnancy has a **25%** chance of sickle cell anaemia. Test the partner of any carrier and offer prenatal diagnosis.
Sickle trait **cannot be seen on a blood count**. β-thalassaemia trait shows a low MCV and MCH, but sickle trait gives normal indices. The lab needs a specific haemoglobinopathy request.

The books differ on the trait. Kumar & Clark and the quick sources call it symptom-free outside extreme hypoxia, while Davidson's warns of a possible higher risk of sudden and cardiovascular death. Follow Davidson's.

sections.title: Clinical features and types of crisis

blocks.text: Severity varies widely: some patients have few symptoms, while others have frequent crises and a shortened life. Between crises, chronic haemolysis causes **pallor, jaundice, pigment gallstones**, a high-output circulation with a **flow murmur**, and delayed growth and puberty.

blocks.title: Childhood clues
items: **Dactylitis** (hand–foot syndrome): painful swelling of the hands and feet in infancy (usually from 4–6 months), often the first sign
The spleen is enlarged in early childhood. Repeated infarcts then shrink it to a fibrotic remnant (**autosplenectomy**), and it is no longer palpable by about 4 years
Children are short but catch up in height by adulthood. They stay underweight, and puberty is often delayed

blocks.title: Types of sickle crisis
rows: Small vessels in active marrow are blocked
Severe bone pain: hands and feet in children; femur, humerus, ribs, pelvis and spine in adults. Fever, tachycardia, sweating. Usually settles in 2–7 days
Infection, fat emboli from infarcted marrow, or pulmonary infarction
Chest pain, dyspnoea, fever, hypoxia and a **new infiltrate on CXR**. Often follows a painful crisis and can kill within hours
Venous outflow from an organ thromboses and blood pools
Children: spleen enlarges rapidly, causing severe anaemia and shock. Adults: liver, with capsular pain
Parvovirus B19 halts red cell production
Profound anaemia that may cause heart failure. Self-limiting, usually within about a week

blocks.title: Causes of an acute fall in Hb from baseline
items: Splenic (or hepatic) sequestration
Marrow aplasia, mostly from parvovirus (erythrovirus) B19
Extra haemolysis from drugs, acute infection or co-existing **G6PD deficiency**

blocks.alt: Algorithm for an acute fall in haemoglobin in sickle cell disease: a low reticulocyte count means aplastic crisis; a high count with a rapidly enlarging spleen or liver means sequestration; otherwise consider extra haemolysis from drugs, infection or G6PD deficiency.

blocks.title: Other acute vaso-occlusive events
items: **Stroke**: the single most devastating complication, mainly in children
**Priapism**: painful, unwanted erection. Most episodes last 30 min–3 h and settle; one lasting **more than 3 hours** is an emergency
**Mesenteric sickling** can mimic an acute abdomen
Triggers include infection, dehydration, cold and major life stress, but crises can also be spontaneous

blocks.note: Look at: CXR in acute chest syndrome. Bilateral lower and mid-zone opacities with mild cardiomegaly.
Look at: body map of sickle complications (stroke, retinopathy, chest syndrome, dactylitis, priapism, leg ulcers, papillary necrosis).

blocks.text: Aplastic crisis is the **only crisis with a low reticulocyte count**. Splenic sequestration also drops the Hb, but the marrow still responds (high retics) and the spleen is large and tender.
Splenic sequestration happens in **children**, whose spleens are still intact. After repeated infarction the adult spleen no longer works, so in adults sequestration affects the **liver**.

blocks.title: Key tests
rows: Compensated anaemia, Hb usually **60–80 g/L**, with reticulocytosis (about 10–20%)
Baseline; repeat daily during a crisis
**Sickle cells, target cells** and features of hyposplenism (e.g. Howell–Jolly bodies) from early childhood
Sickle cells are seen even outside a crisis
HbS gives a **turbid** solution; HbA stays clear
Rapid screen in ED or before surgery. **Cannot tell trait from disease**
HbSS: **no HbA**, HbF 2–20%, the rest HbS
Definitive test; both parents show trait
High flow velocity in large intracranial arteries
Identifies high stroke risk: offer transfusion or hydroxycarbamide

blocks.title: Screening
items: Newborn heel-prick test (around day 5) or cord blood
Antenatal testing of at-risk women, with partner testing and prenatal diagnosis for at-risk couples
Pre-operative testing of people from high-prevalence areas

blocks.title: Work-up in an acute painful crisis
items: All patients: FBC, reticulocytes, U&E, repeated daily
As indicated: LFTs, blood and urine cultures, CXR, ABG if SpO2 < 95%, abdominal ultrasound
Examine the **chest daily** for acute chest syndrome and the **abdomen** for an enlarging liver or spleen (sequestration)

blocks.note: Look at: blood film with crescent-shaped sickle cells (arrowed) and target cells.
Look at: electrophoresis patterns. Trait shows both HbA and HbS bands; sickle cell anaemia shows HbS and HbF with no HbA band.
Look at: (A) sickle cells; (B) Howell–Jolly bodies, a sign of functional hyposplenism.

blocks.text: A positive **solubility (dithionite) test** only shows that HbS is present. It is positive in both trait and disease, so **electrophoresis is always needed** to confirm the diagnosis.
First Aid frames it as: best initial test is FBC with film (reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin, sickle cells); most accurate test is **Hb electrophoresis**.

blocks.title: Chronic complications by system
rows: **Stroke or silent stroke in 10–15% of children**; TIA, fits, cerebral haemorrhage. Typical lesion: distal internal carotid or proximal middle cerebral artery. Silent MRI infarcts are linked to poor school performance

Acute chest syndrome; **pulmonary hypertension** (an independent predictor of death, driven by vasculopathy, repeated chest crises, thromboembolism and nitric oxide loss from haemolysis); chronic lung disease
Functional asplenia: pneumococcus, Haemophilus, meningococcus; osteomyelitis (Staph. aureus, Salmonella)
Avascular necrosis of hips and shoulders, vertebral collapse, short bones of the hands and feet, osteoporosis
Sickle nephropathy (see pearl), papillary necrosis, haematuria, CKD
Background and proliferative retinopathy, vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment: yearly eye checks
Cardiomegaly, high-output failure, arrhythmias, iron-overload cardiomyopathy
Leg ulcers over the malleoli; recurrent priapism leading to impotence

blocks.text: **Sickle nephropathy**: the vasa recta of the medulla are hypoxic and hypertonic, so cells sickle there. The **earliest sign is loss of concentrating ability with polyuria**. Distal RTA and impaired K+ excretion are also typical, and papillary necrosis can occur. Response to erythropoietin is poor.

blocks.title: Pregnancy
items: More painful crises, infections and severe anaemia in the mother
Placental failure: **pre-eclampsia** and **intrauterine growth restriction**
Higher risk of thrombosis, miscarriage and fetal death

blocks.text: **Prognosis (Davidson's)**: even with standard care, about **15% die by age 20** and **50% by age 40**. In Africa, few children with sickle-cell anaemia reach adulthood without medical care. Davidson's names **sickle chest syndrome** as the commonest cause of death in adults.
Osteomyelitis: **Salmonella** is the classic association, but **Staph. aureus** is still the commonest cause overall, with Salmonella second.

Prognosis figures differ. Step-Up quotes a US median survival of about 58 years, with acute chest syndrome and multi-organ failure as the main causes of death. Kumar & Clark adds pulmonary hypertension and chronic lung disease as leading killers. Use Davidson's figures (15% by 20, 50% by 40; chest syndrome).

blocks.title: Long-term care for every patient
items: **Daily folic acid** (chronic haemolysis)
Manage the hyposplenic state: **life-long penicillin V 500 mg twice daily** (a macrolide if allergic)
Vaccines: pneumococcal (re-immunise at least every 5 years), Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcal, and **annual influenza**
Carry an alert card or bracelet; teach the risk of overwhelming sepsis
Avoid precipitants (stay hydrated and warm, avoid high altitude) and treat fever promptly, with a low threshold for antibiotics

blocks.title: Acute painful (vaso-occlusive) crisis
rows: **Aggressive rehydration**: oral about 60 mL/kg/24 h, IV or NG if intake is inadequate

Usually opioids. **Morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV/SC every 20 min** until controlled, then 0.05–0.1 mg/kg every 2–4 h, or PCA. Add paracetamol or an NSAID (avoid NSAIDs in renal impairment); give routine laxatives
Davidson's gives both. Kumar & Clark gives them only when indicated (e.g. O2 if SpO2 < 95%)
Pain, sedation, vital signs and SpO2 every 30 min until stable

blocks.title: Acute chest syndrome
items: Start analgesia, **high-flow oxygen** and antibiotics (**cefotaxime + clarithromycin**) at once, covering pneumococcus, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia
Hydration and incentive spirometry; bronchodilators may help
**Exchange transfusion** if not improving
CPAP/NIV or intubation if ventilation fails

blocks.title: Transfusion: when and how
rows: Steady-state anaemia, minor surgery, uncomplicated painful crisis
Life-threatening crisis (e.g. worsening chest syndrome); preparing for surgery
**Exchange transfusion** (venesect and transfuse at the same time)
Stroke, high-risk transcranial Doppler, recurrent chest syndrome
Match for Rh and Kell, ideally fully genotyped, to limit alloimmunisation; CMV-negative in pregnancy

blocks.title: Disease-modifying and curative treatment
items: **Hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea)**: raises HbF and cuts pain episodes, chest syndrome and transfusion need. Davidson's uses it for recurrent severe crises; Kumar & Clark offers it to almost all patients from 12 months
Hydroxycarbamide is teratogenic and myelosuppressive, so **monitor the blood count** (neutropenia)

**Allogeneic stem cell transplant from an HLA-matched sibling** is potentially curative. The best candidates are young patients with severe complications (stroke, recurrent chest syndrome, refractory pain)

blocks.title: Other emergencies and admission triggers
items: Splenic sequestration: fluid resuscitation and transfusion; consider splenectomy after recurrent episodes
Priapism: a urological emergency, treated by **aspirating blood** from the penis

Admit for: pain not controlled by non-opioids, chest syndrome or pneumonia, splenic or hepatic sequestration, CNS deficit, mesenteric sickling, cholecystitis, arrhythmia, papillary necrosis, hyphaema or retinal detachment, priapism

blocks.title: Pregnancy in sickle-cell disease (Davidson's Box 23.39)
rows: High dose, **5 mg daily**, before and throughout pregnancy
Counsel, update vaccines, test the partner, exclude pulmonary hypertension
LMWH for at least 10 days after vaginal delivery, 6 weeks after caesarean

blocks.text: Oxygen and antibiotics in a painful crisis: Davidson's gives them routinely with fluids and analgesia, while Kumar & Clark gives them only if specifically indicated. Follow Davidson's.

Penicillin prophylaxis: US sources (Step-Up, First Aid) stop it at age 5. Davidson's gives it **life-long** for the hyposplenic state, and Kumar & Clark Essentials lists daily penicillin as routine care with no age cut-off. Follow Davidson's.
Transfuse for a clinical indication, **not for a number**: steady-state Hb of 60–80 g/L is normal for HbSS and is not treated with blood.

cards.front: Molecular defect producing HbS?
cards.back: Point mutation (A→T) giving **valine instead of glutamic acid at position 6** of the β-globin chain

cards.front: Why does sickle cell disease not show before about 6 months of age?
cards.back: Infants make mostly **HbF (α2γ2)**, which has no β chains and does not sickle

cards.front: Why is the sickle gene common where falciparum malaria is endemic?
cards.back: Heterozygotes (HbAS) are protected from dying of falciparum malaria in childhood: a **balanced polymorphism**

cards.front: How does a sickle cell become irreversibly sickled?
cards.back: K+ and water leave via the calcium-activated **Gardos channel**, giving a dense, dehydrated cell that stays sickled when re-oxygenated

cards.front: Which haemoglobin strongly inhibits HbS polymerisation?
cards.back: **HbF**. A high HbF means a milder course; HbC, by contrast, joins polymers more readily than HbA

cards.front: Precipitants of sickling?
cards.back: Hypoxia, infection, dehydration, acidosis, cold ("HIDe in the COLD")

cards.front: HbSC disease vs HbSS?
cards.back: Milder, with fewer crises, but **more retinopathy and thrombosis**, including complications in pregnancy

cards.front: Blood count and film in sickle cell trait?
cards.back: **Normal**. Symptoms only with extreme hypoxia; diagnose with a sickle test or electrophoresis

cards.front: Both parents have sickle trait. Risk per pregnancy of sickle cell anaemia?
cards.back: **25%** (autosomal recessive)

cards.front: Commonest type of sickle crisis, and where is the pain in adults?
cards.back: **Painful vaso-occlusive crisis**: femur, humerus, ribs, pelvis, vertebrae (hands and feet in children)

cards.front: Reticulocyte count in aplastic crisis, and the usual cause?
cards.back: **Low** (unlike every other crisis); **parvovirus B19**

cards.front: Acute chest syndrome: definition and causes?
cards.back: Fever and/or respiratory symptoms with a **new CXR infiltrate**; caused by infection, marrow fat embolism or pulmonary infarction

cards.front: Limitation of the sickle solubility (dithionite) test?
cards.back: Detects HbS but **cannot distinguish trait from disease**; confirm with Hb electrophoresis

cards.front: Hb electrophoresis in HbSS (Davidson's)?
cards.back: No HbA, HbF 2–20%, mostly HbS

cards.front: Stroke in children with SCD: frequency and screening test?
cards.back: Stroke or silent stroke in **10–15%**; screen with **transcranial Doppler** (high velocity = high risk)

cards.front: Earliest renal abnormality in sickle nephropathy?
cards.back: **Loss of urine concentrating ability with polyuria** (sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic vasa recta)

cards.front: Prognosis of HbSS with standard care (Davidson's)?
cards.back: About **15% dead by 20** and **50% by 40**

cards.front: Infection prophylaxis for hyposplenism (Davidson's)?
cards.back: Life-long **penicillin V 500 mg twice daily**, pneumococcal vaccine at least 5-yearly, annual influenza vaccine, alert card

cards.front: Target HbS level on a regular transfusion programme (e.g. after stroke)?
cards.back: **Below 30%**

cards.front: Pregnancy: hydroxycarbamide and aspirin advice?
cards.back: Stop hydroxycarbamide **3 months before conception**; aspirin **75 mg** throughout; folic acid 5 mg daily

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the molecular basis of haemoglobin S for a genetics tutorial.
questions.leadIn: Which change produces haemoglobin S?
options: Lysine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain
Valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain
Deletion of two of the four α-globin genes
Reduced synthesis of structurally normal β chains
Valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the α chain
questions.explanation: HbS comes from a single-base change (A→T) in the β-globin gene, which puts **valine in place of glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain**. The β chain is affected, so the disease appears only once HbF falls.
whyNot: This is HbC: the same position, but lysine is the substituted amino acid.
Gene deletion is how α-thalassaemia arises, a quantitative defect.
Reduced production of normal chains is β-thalassaemia, not a structural variant.
The sickle mutation affects the β chain, not the α chain.

questions.stem: A couple of West African origin, both known carriers of sickle trait, ask why their baby, who has HbSS on newborn screening, is completely well at 3 months of age.
questions.leadIn: What is the best explanation?
options: The infant still makes mainly fetal haemoglobin, which lacks β chains
Maternal antibodies prevent sickling in early infancy
The neonatal spleen removes sickled cells efficiently
HbS does not polymerise until red cells mature in adulthood
Neonatal blood has a higher oxygen tension than adult blood
questions.explanation: HbF is α2γ2 and contains **no β chains**. Defects of the β chain therefore stay hidden until HbF has fallen to adult levels, at **about 6 months**. Dactylitis often follows from about 4–6 months.
whyNot: Maternal antibodies have no role in preventing HbS polymerisation.
The infant spleen is large and still working, but this does not stop sickling. Splenic sequestration is in fact a crisis of young children.
HbS polymerises on deoxygenation at any age once it is the main haemoglobin.
There is no protective rise in oxygen tension in infancy; the protection comes from HbF.

questions.stem: A haematology lecturer shows a film of dense sickle cells that stay sickled even after the sample is oxygenated.
questions.leadIn: Which process mainly explains why these cells stay sickled?
options: Loss of potassium and water through the calcium-activated Gardos channel
Oxidation of haemoglobin to form Heinz bodies
Loss of membrane spectrin from an inherited defect
Antibody coating of the red cells
questions.explanation: Repeated sickling lets **K+ and water escape via the Gardos channel**. The dehydrated, dense cell concentrates HbS and loses membrane flexibility, so it no longer unsickles when oxygenated.
whyNot: Complement-mediated lysis is the mechanism in PNH, not sickling.
Heinz bodies come from oxidant damage in G6PD deficiency.
Inherited cytoskeletal defects cause hereditary spherocytosis.
Antibody coating is the mechanism of autoimmune haemolysis.

questions.stem: Two brothers both have HbSS. The younger has had three admissions in his life; the older has several painful crises a year and has had chest syndrome.
questions.leadIn: Which laboratory feature best explains the younger brother's milder course?
questions.explanation: **HbF strongly inhibits HbS polymerisation**, so patients with a high HbF have few crises. This is why hydroxycarbamide, which raises HbF, helps.
whyNot: A higher reticulocyte count reflects more haemolysis, not milder disease.
A lower Hb does not protect against sickling.
More HbS per cell makes tactoids form more easily, which worsens disease.
G6PD deficiency adds haemolysis and can cause an acute fall in Hb.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman of Ghanaian origin, 30 weeks pregnant, has had only two painful crises in her life. She has proliferative retinopathy and now has a deep vein thrombosis. Electrophoresis shows HbS and HbC bands with no HbA.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HbS plus HbC with no HbA is **HbSC disease**. It is milder, with fewer crises, but brings **more retinopathy and thrombosis**, especially in pregnancy.
whyNot: HbSS shows no HbC band and usually has many more crises.
Trait has an HbA band and no retinopathy or thrombosis risk of this kind.
S/β-thalassaemia behaves like HbSS and has no HbC band.
HbC trait has HbA and is clinically silent.

questions.stem: A fit 22-year-old Nigerian student has a positive sickle solubility test before a dental procedure. He has never been unwell, and electrophoresis shows both HbA and HbS.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is most likely on his full blood count and film?
options: Low MCV and MCH with target cells
questions.explanation: This is **sickle cell trait (HbAS)**. The count and film are **normal**, unlike thalassaemia trait. Symptoms arise only with extreme hypoxia.
whyNot: Compensated anaemia at 60–80 g/L with reticulocytosis is HbSS.
Low MCV and MCH suggest thalassaemia trait, not sickle trait.
Sickle cells and hyposplenic features are found in HbSS.
Spherocytes suggest hereditary spherocytosis or immune haemolysis.

questions.theme: Acute presentations in sickle cell disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

items.stem: A 9-month-old boy with HbSS is irritable and won't use his hands. Both hands and feet are swollen, warm and tender over their backs. Temperature 38.0 °C.
items.explanation: Painful swelling of the hands and feet in infancy is **dactylitis**, the vaso-occlusive crisis of small bones in a young child and often the first sign of the disease.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man admitted with a femoral pain crisis develops pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness on day 2. SpO2 is 89% on air, and a new left lower zone infiltrate is seen on the chest film.
items.explanation: Chest pain, hypoxia and a **new CXR infiltrate**, arising after a bone crisis (marrow fat embolism), is **acute chest syndrome**. It can kill within hours.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man with HbSS has had a painful erection for 4 hours that has not settled with fluids or emptying his bladder.
items.explanation: Vaso-occlusion in the corpora causes **priapism**. Lasting more than 3 hours makes it an emergency, and recurrent episodes risk impotence.

questions.theme: Choosing an investigation in sickle cell disease
questions.leadIn: For each situation below, choose the most appropriate investigation from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man from Sierra Leone needs an emergency appendicectomy tonight. His sickle status is unknown and theatre wants a rapid screen for HbS.
items.explanation: The **solubility test** gives a quick yes/no for HbS before surgery or in the ED. It cannot separate trait from disease, so electrophoresis must follow.

items.stem: The test above is positive. The surgical team now needs to know whether he has sickle cell trait or sickle cell disease.
items.explanation: Two steps: the screen is positive in both trait and disease, so you need a test that quantifies each haemoglobin. That is **Hb electrophoresis** (HbSS: no HbA, HbF 2–20%, mostly HbS).

items.stem: A well 6-year-old girl with HbSS attends routine clinic. Her parents ask how her risk of stroke can be assessed.
items.explanation: **Transcranial Doppler** measures flow velocity in the large intracranial arteries. A high velocity means high stroke risk and prompts a transfusion programme or hydroxycarbamide.

items.stem: A 7-year-old with HbSS has a haemoglobin of 45 g/L (baseline 75 g/L) a week after a febrile illness with a rash. The spleen is not palpable.
items.explanation: Distinguish aplastic crisis from sequestration or extra haemolysis with the **reticulocyte count**. Low reticulocytes after a viral illness point to parvovirus B19 aplasia.

questions.theme: Chronic complications of sickle cell disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy with HbSS still wets the bed and drinks large volumes. Early-morning urine osmolality is low despite overnight fluid restriction. Creatinine is normal.
items.explanation: Sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic vasa recta first causes **loss of concentrating ability and polyuria**, the earliest sign of sickle nephropathy.

items.stem: A 10-year-old girl with HbSS and no history of stroke has falling school grades. MRI shows small deep white-matter infarcts, and neurological examination is normal.
items.explanation: Infarcts seen on MRI without any clinical event are **silent infarcts**. They are common in children with SCD and linked to poor educational attainment.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with HbSS has had recurrent right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Ultrasound shows multiple small dark stones.
items.explanation: Chronic haemolysis raises the bilirubin load, which forms **pigment gallstones**. These can cause biliary colic and cholecystitis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with HbSS has worsening exertional breathlessness. Echo shows a raised pulmonary artery pressure with right ventricular dilatation; he has had several chest crises.
items.explanation: **Pulmonary hypertension** follows vasculopathy, repeated chest crises, thromboembolism and nitric oxide loss from haemolysis. It is an independent predictor of death and should prompt therapy to lower HbS.

questions.theme: Transfusion decisions in sickle cell disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most appropriate blood-product strategy from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Regular transfusion programme keeping HbS below 30%

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with HbSS, steady-state Hb 72 g/L, is admitted with a typical rib and back pain crisis. She is not hypoxic and her chest is clear. Her Hb today is 70 g/L.
items.explanation: Steady-state anaemia and an **uncomplicated painful crisis** are not indications for blood. Treat with fluids and analgesia.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy with HbSS is pale and drowsy with a left upper quadrant mass that has grown over 6 hours. Hb is 38 g/L and reticulocytes are high.
items.explanation: Acute **splenic sequestration** needs volume replacement and a **simple top-up** transfusion.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with acute chest syndrome is on high-flow oxygen, cefotaxime and clarithromycin, but over 12 hours his SpO2 falls and both lungs become involved.
items.explanation: Acute chest syndrome that is **not improving** is life-threatening. **Exchange transfusion** (venesect and transfuse at the same time) replaces HbS with HbA quickly.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl with HbSS recovered from a left middle cerebral artery stroke last month.
items.explanation: After stroke (secondary prevention), a **regular transfusion programme** suppresses HbS production and keeps HbS below 30%.

questions.leadIn: For each person below, choose the most likely haemoglobin genotype from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 2-year-old has had episodes of swollen hands. Hb is 68 g/L with high reticulocytes. Electrophoresis shows no HbA, about 10% HbF and the rest HbS. Both parents show HbA and HbS.
items.explanation: No HbA, HbF 2–20% and predominant HbS, with both parents carriers, is **HbSS**.

items.stem: A pregnant 25-year-old from Jamaica has a normal FBC and film. A specifically requested haemoglobinopathy screen shows HbA and HbS bands.
items.explanation: Both HbA and HbS with a normal count and film is **sickle cell trait**. It is invisible on the FBC, so it needs a specific request.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has severe disease like HbSS, with frequent crises. His mother has HbA and HbS; his father has a low MCV and MCH with no HbS.
items.explanation: Two steps: he inherited HbS from his mother. His father's microcytosis without HbS suggests β-thalassaemia trait. Together these give **HbS/β-thalassaemia**, which behaves clinically like HbSS.

items.stem: A healthy 40-year-old man has microcytosis with a low MCH. He has had no response to iron and his ferritin is normal. Electrophoresis shows a raised HbA2 and no HbS.
items.explanation: Microcytosis that does not respond to iron, with a **raised HbA2** and no variant band, fits **β-thalassaemia trait**. That is the contrast with sickle trait, which has normal indices.

questions.leadIn: For each observation below, choose the mechanism that best explains it. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Inhibition of HbS polymerisation by HbF
Easier release of oxygen to the tissues by HbS
Sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic vasa recta
Fat embolism from infarcted bone marrow
Venous outflow thrombosis causing organ pooling
Potassium loss through the Gardos channel

items.stem: A 25-year-old man with HbSS and an Hb of 70 g/L plays five-a-side football weekly without breathlessness.
items.explanation: HbS **gives up oxygen to the tissues more readily** than HbA, so patients tolerate 60–80 g/L well.

items.stem: A 12-year-old with HbSS has had far fewer crises since starting a daily oral cytotoxic tablet two years ago.
items.explanation: Hydroxycarbamide **raises HbF**, which inhibits polymerisation and reduces crises and chest syndrome.

items.stem: A 20-year-old with sickle trait passes large volumes of dilute urine and cannot concentrate it on a water-deprivation test.
items.explanation: Even trait cells sickle in the **hypoxic, hypertonic medulla**, damaging the vasa recta and the concentrating mechanism (isosthenuria).

items.stem: A 4-year-old with HbSS develops pneumococcal meningitis despite having had a large spleen as a toddler. The spleen can no longer be felt.
items.explanation: Repeated splenic infarcts cause **functional asplenia (autosplenectomy)**, which leaves the child open to encapsulated organisms.

questions.stem: A clinical tutor asks which complication Davidson's names as the leading killer of adults with sickle-cell disease.
questions.leadIn: Which is the best answer?
questions.explanation: Davidson's names **sickle chest syndrome** as the commonest cause of death in adults. Stroke is the most devastating complication but mainly affects children.
whyNot: Stroke is the most devastating complication but occurs mainly in children.
Splenic sequestration is a crisis of young children, before autosplenectomy.
Only a minority develop ESRD.
Overwhelming sepsis is a risk, especially in children, but is not named as the leading adult cause.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with HbSS has a high flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery on routine transcranial Doppler. He is neurologically normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start a regular transfusion programme to keep HbS below 30%
questions.explanation: High Doppler velocity means a **high stroke risk**. Primary prevention is a **regular transfusion programme** (or hydroxycarbamide), keeping HbS below 30%.
whyNot: Antiplatelet therapy is not the strategy for preventing sickle stroke in these sources.
Waiting ignores a high immediate risk.
Anticoagulation does not address the sickle vasculopathy.
Splenectomy is for recurrent sequestration, not stroke prevention.

questions.theme: Causes of an acute fall in haemoglobin in sickle cell disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl with HbSS is breathless and pale a week after a febrile viral illness. Hb is 42 g/L (baseline 78 g/L), reticulocytes are almost absent, and there is no organomegaly.
items.explanation: Step 1: a big Hb drop. Step 2: the reticulocytes are **low**, unlike every other crisis, so the marrow has stopped. Step 3: a recent viral illness fits **parvovirus B19**, which invades erythroid progenitors. This is an aplastic crisis; give a top-up transfusion until the marrow recovers.

items.stem: A 2-year-old boy with HbSS becomes suddenly pale and cold with a fast pulse. His spleen, previously just palpable, now reaches the umbilicus. Hb 35 g/L; reticulocytes high.
items.explanation: Step 1: shock with a rapidly enlarging spleen. Step 2: a high reticulocyte count shows the marrow is working, so the blood has pooled rather than not been made. Step 3: his age (spleen still intact) fits **splenic sequestration**. Resuscitate and give a top-up transfusion.

items.stem: A 27-year-old Nigerian man with HbSS develops dark urine and a fall in Hb from 80 to 55 g/L, two days after starting an oxidant antimalarial drug. Reticulocytes are high, and the spleen and liver are not enlarged.
items.explanation: Step 1: the fall comes with a working marrow (high retics) and no organ enlargement, so it is not aplasia or sequestration. Step 2: an oxidant drug trigger points to extra haemolysis from **co-existing G6PD deficiency**, a recognised cause of an acute Hb fall in sickle patients.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with HbSS arrives with 6 hours of severe pain in his thighs and lower back, unrelieved by paracetamol and ibuprofen at home. He weighs 70 kg and is opioid-naive. SpO2 is 97% on air, and his chest and abdomen are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which analgesic plan is most appropriate?
options: Morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV or SC every 20 minutes until the pain is controlled
Continue oral paracetamol and ibuprofen only
Wait for an exchange transfusion to relieve the pain
questions.explanation: Step 1: pain not controlled by non-opioids means **admission**. Step 2: strong opioids are needed, and **morphine is the drug of choice**: 0.1 mg/kg IV/SC every 20 min until controlled, then 2–4-hourly or by PCA. Step 3: add paracetamol or an NSAID, laxatives, fluids, oxygen and antibiotics (Davidson's), and incentive spirometry.
whyNot: Non-opioids have already failed, which is itself an admission criterion.
A single weak opioid dose will not control a sickle crisis; titrated morphine is recommended.
Transfusion is not indicated for an uncomplicated painful crisis.
A once-daily weak opioid is too slow and too weak for a severe crisis.

questions.theme: Drug therapy in sickle cell disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most appropriate drug from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 17-year-old with HbSS has had five admissions with painful crises and two episodes of acute chest syndrome this year. A drug is needed to reduce future events.
items.explanation: **Hydroxycarbamide** raises HbF and reduces painful crises, chest syndrome and transfusion need. Monitor the blood count for neutropenia.

items.stem: A 21-year-old with HbSS has a fever, cough, hypoxia and a new right lower zone infiltrate.
items.explanation: Acute chest syndrome needs immediate antibiotics covering pneumococcus and atypical organisms: **cefotaxime plus clarithromycin**.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with HbSS is 12 weeks pregnant. Which drug should she take throughout pregnancy to reduce the risk of placental failure?
items.explanation: Davidson's Box 23.39: **aspirin 75 mg** throughout pregnancy, because pre-eclampsia and growth restriction are more common.

items.stem: A 19-year-old with HbSS moves to an adult clinic. He asks which daily tablet will protect him against overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis.
items.explanation: Hyposplenism needs life-long **penicillin V 500 mg twice daily** (a macrolide if allergic), plus vaccines.

questions.theme: Genetic risk in sickle cell families
questions.leadIn: For each question below, choose the correct probability from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: Both partners have sickle cell trait (HbAS). What is the chance that their next child has sickle cell anaemia?
items.explanation: AS × AS gives ¼ AA, ½ AS and ¼ SS, so the risk is **25%** for each pregnancy.

items.stem: A man with HbSS and a woman with normal haemoglobin (HbAA) have a child. What is the chance that the child has sickle cell trait?
items.explanation: Every child receives an S from the father and an A from the mother, so all are **AS (100%)**, and none has the disease.

items.stem: A man with HbSS and a woman with sickle trait have a child. What is the chance that the child has sickle cell anaemia?
items.explanation: SS × AS: the father always passes S, and the mother passes S half the time, so **50%** of children are SS.

items.stem: Two carriers have an unaffected (not HbSS) child. What is the chance that this child is a carrier?
items.explanation: Two steps: of AS × AS offspring, SS is excluded. That leaves AA (1 part) and AS (2 parts), so the chance of being a carrier is **2/3 (67%)**.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with HbSS is moving from paediatric to adult care. He was told as a child that he could stop daily penicillin after the age of 5, but his paediatrician kept it going. He asks whether he can stop now.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson's, what is the best advice?
options: Continue penicillin V 500 mg twice daily for life
Stop penicillin now, as protection is needed only under 5 years
Switch to antibiotics only during crises
Stop penicillin once pneumococcal vaccination is complete
Replace penicillin with monthly intramuscular immunoglobulin
questions.explanation: All patients with sickle-cell disease are functionally hyposplenic. Davidson's advises **life-long penicillin V 500 mg twice daily** with pneumococcal re-immunisation at least 5-yearly and annual influenza vaccine. US sources limiting it to under-5s are the exam trap.
whyNot: This is the US approach (Step-Up, First Aid); Davidson's takes precedence.
Overwhelming sepsis can strike at any time, not only during crises.
Vaccines supplement penicillin but do not replace it.
Immunoglobulin is not part of hyposplenism prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with HbSS wants to start a family. She takes hydroxycarbamide for recurrent crises and ramipril for microalbuminuria.
questions.leadIn: Which piece of pre-conception advice is correct?
options: Stop hydroxycarbamide 3 months before trying to conceive
Continue hydroxycarbamide throughout pregnancy to prevent crises
Continue ramipril to protect her kidneys
Avoid aspirin in pregnancy because of bleeding risk
questions.explanation: Davidson's Box 23.39: **stop hydroxycarbamide 3 months before conception** (it is teratogenic), stop ACE inhibitors, take **folic acid 5 mg** daily, and give aspirin 75 mg throughout pregnancy.
whyNot: Hydroxycarbamide is teratogenic and must be stopped before conception.
The high dose, 5 mg daily, is recommended in SCD.
ACE inhibitors should be stopped before conception.
Aspirin 75 mg is recommended throughout pregnancy to reduce placental failure.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with HbSS presents with a fever of 39 °C, cough and pleuritic chest pain. SpO2 is 90% on air and a new right middle zone opacity is seen.
questions.leadIn: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: This is **acute chest syndrome**. Start antibiotics covering pneumococcus and atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) at once, e.g. **cefotaxime plus clarithromycin**, with high-flow O2 and analgesia. Exchange transfuse if not improving.
whyNot: Oral amoxicillin alone misses atypical organisms and is not enough for a life-threatening syndrome.
Flucloxacillin covers staphylococci but not pneumococcus reliably or atypicals.
Metronidazole covers anaerobes only.
Nitrofurantoin is a urinary antiseptic.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely organism from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 9-year-old with HbSS has 5 days of fever and a hot, very tender distal femur. MRI shows marrow oedema with a subperiosteal collection. Which organism is statistically the most common cause?
items.explanation: Salmonella is the classic association, but **Staph. aureus is still the most common cause** of osteomyelitis in SCD, with Salmonella second.

items.stem: A 5-year-old with HbSS who has not taken his penicillin for months becomes septic within hours, with purpura and hypotension. Gram-positive diplococci grow in the blood culture.
items.explanation: Functional asplenia leaves patients exposed to encapsulated bacteria. Gram-positive diplococci are **Strep. pneumoniae**, which is why penicillin and pneumococcal vaccination matter.

items.stem: A 6-year-old with HbSS has a profound anaemia with almost no reticulocytes, a week after a mild febrile illness.
items.explanation: A low-reticulocyte crisis is aplasia, caused by **parvovirus B19** infecting erythroid progenitors.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman of Ghanaian origin attends antenatal booking. Her full blood count is normal (MCV 88 fL, MCH 30 pg). The midwife says this rules out a haemoglobinopathy.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis or a specific sickle screen
Reassure her that sickle trait has been excluded
Repeat the full blood count at 28 weeks
Refer for chorionic villus sampling straight away
questions.explanation: **Sickle trait cannot be detected on a blood count**: indices and film are normal, unlike β-thalassaemia trait. The lab needs a specific request (electrophoresis or sickle test). If she is a carrier, test her partner.
whyNot: A normal FBC does not exclude sickle trait.
Ferritin assesses iron stores, not haemoglobin variants.
A repeat FBC will be normal again in trait.
Fetal testing is offered only once both parents are known carriers.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with HbSS has a normal creatinine and no proteinuria, but his mother notes he passes large volumes of urine day and night.
questions.leadIn: Which renal abnormality is the earliest to develop in sickle nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Red cells sickle in the hypoxic, hypertonic vasa recta. The **earliest change is loss of concentrating ability with polyuria**. Distal RTA and impaired potassium excretion (a tendency to high, not low, K+) are also typical, papillary necrosis can occur, and a minority reach ESRD.
whyNot: Heavy proteinuria is not the earliest change.
Potassium excretion is impaired, so hyperkalaemia is the tendency, not hypokalaemia.
Haematuria in SCD is usually from papillary necrosis or infarction, and it is not the first change.
A fall in GFR is late, occurring in a minority.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with HbSS needs a regular exchange transfusion programme after a stroke. The blood bank asks how to reduce his risk of red cell alloimmunisation.
questions.leadIn: Which blood-matching policy is most appropriate?
options: Match for Rh and Kell antigens, ideally with full genotyping
Match for ABO and RhD only
Match for HLA class I antigens
Use any ABO-compatible blood that has been irradiated
Use group O RhD-negative blood for every transfusion
questions.explanation: Donor–recipient ethnic mismatch makes alloantibodies common. Red cells should be **matched for Rh and Kell**, and ideally patients are **fully genotyped** before their first transfusion.
whyNot: ABO/RhD matching alone leaves a high risk of alloimmunisation to other Rh and Kell antigens.
HLA matching is for platelets or transplant, not red cell alloimmunisation.
Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated GvHD, not alloimmunisation.
O-negative blood does not address Kell or other Rh antigens.

ospe.identify: Blood film: crescent-shaped **sickle cells** (arrowed) and **target cells**. Diagnosis: sickle cell anaemia (HbSS).
Film: sickle cells (arrowed) plus target ("Mexican hat") cells. Diagnosis: sickle cell disease.
(A) Sickle-shaped red cells; (B) **Howell–Jolly bodies**, a sign of functional hyposplenism or asplenia.
Hb electrophoresis: **trait** shows both HbA and HbS bands; **sickle cell anaemia** shows HbS and HbF with **no HbA** band; β-thalassaemia major is mainly HbF.
CXR: bilateral lower and mid-zone opacities with mild cardiomegaly in a young sickle patient with chest pain. This is **acute chest syndrome**.
Composite figure: the film shows sickle cells and a **nucleated red cell**; the electrophoresis gel separates HbA, HbS, HbC and HbF; the body map lists the organ complications.
Peripheral smear: numerous elongated, crescent-shaped **sickled red cells**. Diagnosis: sickle cell disease.
